items.title: What design actually is
items.description: A friendly first look at the job behind the job.

metadata.youllNeed: A notes app or paper. That's it.
metadata.practise: Teardown one app you use daily (Stage 01 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: What is design, really? A friendly beginner's guide
metadata.seoDescription: Design isn't just making things pretty. It's making deliberate choices so something works better for a person. A clear, no-jargon introduction for beginners.

quiz.question: Which sentence describes design best?
options: Making deliberate choices so something works better for a person
quiz.why: Looks matter, but design is about solving a problem for someone.

quiz.question: What makes a decision a design decision?
options: It's made in a design tool
It changes how someone experiences or uses something
quiz.why: Design decisions are about the effect on the person using the thing, not the tool or the job title.

quiz.question: Why do designers care about constraints?
options: They remove the need for research
They're the material a designer actually works with
quiz.why: Constraints are the raw material. Without them, design becomes decoration.

items.title: UX vs UI vs Product
items.description: Same job, different job titles, and why the difference actually matters.

metadata.youllNeed: No tools. Just your brain and maybe a notebook.
metadata.practise: Open one app and write down three UX decisions, three UI decisions and one product decision it contains.
metadata.seoTitle: UX vs UI vs Product Design: What's the Difference?
metadata.seoDescription: UX, UI and product design explained without jargon. Learn what each role actually does, where they overlap, and which one fits the work you want to do.

quiz.question: What is the core focus of UX design?
options: How the product works and feels over time
quiz.why: UX is about the experience of using the product: the flow, the logic, the friction points and how it feels across the whole journey.

quiz.question: Which of these is a UI decision?
options: Deciding the onboarding flow should have three steps
Choosing a 16px font size for body text
Deciding to build a mobile app instead of a website
Choosing not to build a feature
quiz.why: Font size, spacing, colour, radius and motion are UI decisions. They shape the surface the user sees and touches.

quiz.question: Which role is closest to owning whether the right thing gets built?
quiz.why: Product design sits closest to the product problem: what to build, for whom, why now, and how it fits the business.

items.title: The design process, start to finish
items.description: The loop designers actually use, without the poster version.

metadata.youllNeed: A real problem you've noticed in an app you use.
metadata.practise: Run the loop on paper once. Pick one screen you use daily and ask what's actually wrong with it.
metadata.seoTitle: The Design Process, Start to Finish (For Beginners)
metadata.seoDescription: A practical guide to the design process: understand, define, sketch, test and refine. Learn how real designers move through a problem without pretending it's linear.

quiz.question: What's the first move in the design process?
options: Understand the problem and the person
quiz.why: You can't design a good answer to a question you haven't understood. Start with the problem and the person.

quiz.question: What does "define" mean in the process?
options: Write a clear problem statement and constraints
Show the work to a client
quiz.why: Define turns a vague mess into a specific problem you can solve and test against.

quiz.question: Why do designers test early?
options: To make the work look finished
To catch wrong assumptions while they're still cheap to fix
To avoid talking to users later
quiz.why: Testing early is about reducing the cost of being wrong. A rough prototype can reveal a bad assumption before you polish it.

items.title: Setting up Figma
items.description: The 30-minute setup that saves you months of mess.

metadata.youllNeed: A free Figma account and a browser. Install the desktop app if you can.
metadata.practise: Set up one project file with pages, a frame and a cover. Nothing fancy.
metadata.seoTitle: How to Set Up Figma as a Beginner (Without Making a Mess)
metadata.seoDescription: A simple Figma setup for beginners: projects, pages, frames, layers and naming. Build habits that keep your files clean from day one.

quiz.question: What should you do before opening Figma?
options: Decide what the file is for and who will use it
quiz.why: A file's purpose and audience decide how it should be organised. Tool setup comes after that.

quiz.question: What's the safest beginner file structure?
options: One page with everything on it
One project per roadmap, one file per project, pages for explore, wireframes and final
A new file for every screen
quiz.why: Separating exploration, wireframes and final work keeps the file understandable and prevents accidental edits.

quiz.question: Why is naming layers important?
options: It makes the file searchable and easier for you and others to navigate
quiz.why: Names are how you and collaborators find things later. A named layer is a decision you don't have to remember.

items.title: Seeing like a designer
items.description: How to notice what everyone else walks past.

metadata.youllNeed: A camera or screenshot tool. A notes app.
metadata.practise: Screenshot five screens you use daily and write one design observation for each.
metadata.seoTitle: How to See Like a Designer: A Beginner's Practice
metadata.seoDescription: Designers notice details other people walk past. Learn a simple daily practice for spotting hierarchy, spacing, contrast and intent in the interfaces around you.

quiz.question: What does 'seeing like a designer' mean?
options: Noticing the choices behind what you're looking at
quiz.why: It's a trained attention to decisions: what was chosen, what was left out, and what effect it has.

quiz.question: What should you look for first when studying a screen?
options: What your eye goes to first and why
quiz.why: Your attention is data. If you notice something first, the design is doing that on purpose (or by accident).

quiz.question: Why is collecting screenshots useful?
options: It builds a reference library you can compare and learn from
It makes you a designer instantly
quiz.why: A reference library lets you spot patterns across products and gives you evidence when you critique or design.

items.title: Giving and taking critique
items.description: How to make feedback useful instead of personal.

metadata.youllNeed: A piece of work you made, and a friend or a notebook.
metadata.practise: Critique one screen using the I notice / I wonder / What if format. Then ask someone to critique yours.
metadata.seoTitle: Giving and Taking Design Critique (Without Taking It Personally)
metadata.seoDescription: Learn how to give useful design feedback and receive critique without defensiveness. A practical framework for beginners and small teams.

quiz.question: What makes critique useful?
options: It's specific and tied to the work, not the person
It's given by a senior designer
quiz.why: Useful critique points to a specific decision and its effect. It gives the maker something to act on.

quiz.question: What should you do first when receiving critique?
options: Explain why the critic is wrong
quiz.why: Listening doesn't mean agreeing. It means understanding the other person's experience before deciding what to do.

quiz.question: Which is a good critique question?
options: What do you notice first, and what do you think this screen is for?
Why did you use that colour?
quiz.why: Open questions about attention and intent surface useful information without putting the maker on the defensive.
